analysis.one_liner: Ends immigration detention and ankle monitors, redirecting money to community nonprofits' housing, legal, and health services.
analysis.headline: Referred to two House committees on January 21, 2026 and to their subcommittees the next day; no hearing or vote has been scheduled, and all 16 cosponsors are Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: Within six months of passage, the Department of Homeland Security would have to release every noncitizen it has detained and remove every ankle monitor; within two years it would have to terminate all detention and monitoring contracts, and federal money could no longer pay for detention, ankle monitors, or information-sharing with state and local police. ICE's operations funding could not be used for arrests, detention, or removals. In their place, the Department of Health and Human Services would run grants to community nonprofits for housing, mental health care, legal help, English classes, and job assistance — services that would be voluntary and off-limits to immigration surveillance or data-sharing.
analysis.who_benefits: Noncitizens in detention, people wearing ankle monitors, and their families and communities. Anyone facing deportation loses the threat of lockup; anyone under electronic monitoring loses the bracelet. Nonprofits that provide immigrant services gain a new federal funding stream.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Homeland Security to release on their own recognizance every noncitizen it has detained, no later than six months after enactment.
Terminates all federal contracts for immigration detention and monitoring within two years, then bans any federal funds for them.
Removes every ankle monitor from noncitizens within six months and bans federal funding for ankle monitoring programs after that.
Bars ICE 'Operations and Support' money from arrests, detention, removals, or processing charging documents, and from helping state or local police enforce status-based offenses.

Ends federal funding for Secure Communities-style information sharing between Homeland Security and state or local police within two years, and repeals the 1996 laws that bar states and localities from restricting such cooperation.

Creates a grant program at Health and Human Services for community nonprofits to provide housing assistance, mental health services, healthcare access, employment help, English classes, education assistance, and immigration legal help.
Requires the services to be opt-in and voluntary, provided without surveillance, and bars grantees from sending anyone's personal information to any federal agency.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that run immigration detention centers and ankle-monitoring programs lose their federal contracts, and the federal government loses nearly all of its civil immigration detention and removal machinery. Supporters say that capacity should not exist; opponents say the public bears the risk of a system with no detention or removal tools at all.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private detention firms and ankle-monitor vendors

drawbacks.text: The bill does not just close detention centers — it repeals the legal authority to detain or remove most noncitizens, including people who have received final removal orders, leaving the government with essentially no civil immigration enforcement tools.
It repeals the deportation grounds for using public benefits (public charge) and for unlawful voting, removing existing rules that even many immigration-reform supporters would keep.
It ends electronic monitoring outright, including for people who were placed on ankle monitors precisely as a less restrictive alternative to detention.
Even a supporter would acknowledge the timeline is abrupt: every detainee released and every ankle monitor removed within six months, with no transition period for courts or agencies to adjust.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is an abolition bill, not a reform bill: it dismantles the entire detention and electronic-monitoring system rather than fixing conditions in it, and it pays for services rather than enforcement. For immigrants currently detained or monitored, the benefits are direct and large. The cost is the near-total elimination of civil immigration enforcement, a step with no precedent and no plan for the cases — like people with final removal orders — that the current system exists to resolve. That design, plus the fact that no Republican supports it, is why it has not moved.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sits with the House Judiciary and Homeland Security committees; after being sent to their border-security and oversight subcommittees on January 22, 2026, no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Delia Ramirez of Illinois introduced the bill on January 21, 2026, joined by five original cosponsors: Reps. Clarke of New York, Velázquez, Davis of Illinois, Lee of Pennsylvania, and Tlaib.
Sixteen Democratic cosponsors had joined by the latest count; no Republican has.

The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Homeland Security Committee, and one day later each sent it to a subcommittee — Oversight, Investigations, and Accountability, and Border Security and Enforcement.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote has taken place since.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has happened, the status quo continues: private detention and electronic-monitoring contractors keep their federal contracts, and the detention and monitoring system operates as before. The immigrants this bill would release remain subject to detention and monitoring, and its supporters have only a record of introduction and referral to show.

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to two committees, where it was sent to subcommittees and has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote since January 22, 2026.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors are Democrats and the sponsor is a Democrat; no Republican has signed on, and the House Republican majority has taken no action to advance it.

industries.industry: Private prison and immigration detention contractors
industries.note: The bill requires Homeland Security to terminate every detention contract within two years and bans all federal funds for detention after that. These companies profit per bed occupied, so their interest runs directly against the people the bill would release.
All ankle monitors must come off within six months and federal funding for monitoring programs ends. The bill replaces a paid-surveillance model with voluntary, surveillance-free services.

The bill creates a new HHS grant stream for nonprofits — barred from any past law-enforcement involvement — to deliver housing, healthcare, legal, education, and employment services, and protects their clients from data-sharing with federal agencies.

analysis.trajectory: With 16 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no movement past subcommittee referral in a House run by the other party, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or a vote before the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027; bills at this stage almost never reach the floor.
